title: Discrete Gaussian Sampling Meets BDGL Decoding: Solving the Shortest Vector Problem in $2^{0.5596n+o(n)}$ Time
authors: Yiming Gao, Yansong Feng, and Honggang Hu
abstract:
Aggarwal, Dadush, Regev, and Stephens-Davidowitz (ADRS) gave a $2^{n+o(n)}$ time algorithm for the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) based on discrete Gaussian sampling (DGS), together with an honest sampler producing $2^{n/2}$ samples above the smoothing parameter in $2^{n/2+o(n)}$ time and space. Gao, Feng, and Hu (GFH) subsequently introduced DGS on random prime-index superlattices, making this sampler available at the shortest vector scale and obtaining a $2^{0.7314n+o(n)}$ time algorithm. In a different direction, the Becker--Ducas--Gama--Laarhoven (BDGL) sieve uses spherical product codes to find correlated pairs and runs in $2^{0.2925n+o(n)}$ time under the random list heuristic.

We combine the random superlattice DGS framework with a single BDGL product code decoding layer. The algorithm splits the DGS output into two lists. For a fixed shortest vector $v$, the Gaussian midpoint identity turns the event $X-Y=v$ into a birthday event, while equal quotient labels certify that the reported difference belongs to the input lattice. The product code decoder locates the corresponding pair without enumerating all pairwise differences.

Our analysis makes no random list assumption. For a fixed shortest vector $v$, once the retained lists contain a pair $x,y$ with $x-y=v$, the BDGL product code finds that pair with high probability. We extend the product code analysis so that this guarantee is compatible with the claimed time and space bounds. A centered quotient line gives a $2^{0.5822n+o(n)}$ time algorithm. We then replace the line through the zero residue with a random affine translate. This lets us target a rarer midpoint shell. As a result, we obtain a randomized classical algorithm for SVP that runs in $2^{0.5596n+o(n)}$ time and uses $2^{n/2+o(n)}$ space.

1     Introduction
Let L ⊂ Rn be a full-rank lattice. Given a basis of L, the Shortest Vector Problem (SVP) asks us to
find a nonzero vector v ∈ L of minimum Euclidean norm:

                                   ∥v∥ = λ1 (L) := min ∥x∥ .
                                                     x∈L\{0}

SVP is a standard benchmark for exponential time lattice algorithms and a basic primitive in lattice
reduction and cryptanalysis. The exact version also connects two algorithmic viewpoints. The first
uses rigorous algorithms with worst-case guarantees. The second uses sieving algorithms whose best
running times are predicted by random-list heuristics.
    On the provable side, Ajtai, Kumar, and Sivakumar initiated randomized sieving with a 2O(n)
algorithm [AKS01]. Subsequent work developed both practical and rigorous variants [NV08, PS09].
Micciancio and Voulgaris later gave a deterministic 22n+o(n) -time algorithm based on Voronoi
cells [MV13]. Aggarwal, Dadush, Regev, and Stephens-Davidowitz (ADRS) reached 2n+o(n) time
and space by reducing SVP to centered discrete Gaussian sampling [ADRSD15].
    The heuristic picture is much more encouraging. Under the random-list assumptions commonly
used in lattice sieving, the Becker–Ducas–Gama–Laarhoven (BDGL) sieve runs in time

                                   (3/2)n/2+o(n) = 20.2925n+o(n)

by using spherical product codes to find correlated pairs [BDGL16]. The large gap between this
heuristic bound and the best rigorous bound naturally raises the following question: can we combine
this pair-finding method with a sampler whose input distribution is rigorously controlled?
    Two ingredients make this question approachable. ADRS gave an honest discrete Gaussian
sampler [ADRSD15]. Above the smoothing parameter, it produces 2n/2 independent samples in
2n/2+o(n) time and space. Gao, Feng, and Hu (GFH) then made this sampler useful at the shortest-
vector scale by sampling from a random prime-index superlattice Γ ⊃ L [GFH26]. At this scale,
the superlattice Γ is smooth, even if L is not. Honest DGS is run on Γ, and each sample is tested
for membership in L. This gives an algorithm using 20.7314n+o(n) time and 2n/2+o(n) space. Each
sampled vector that falls in L is a direct chance to recover a shortest vector.
    Our starting point is to use the samples in pairs. The GFH algorithm looks for a direct hit: it
samples X ∼ DΓ,t until X is a shortest vector of L. Thus, a list of N samples gives N chances. In
contrast, the same list gives N (N − 1) ordered differences. This suggests replacing

                       direct hit: X = v     with       pair hit: X − Y = v.

take quadratic time and remove the gain. Instead, we use the BDGL product code decoder on a

The DGS analysis supplies the endpoint distribution, radial concentration, and target pair correlation.
The product code analysis supplies the cap and wedge probabilities needed to search that distribution.
Equal labels make every reported difference a lattice vector, so the algorithm can return the shortest
nonzero difference it reports.

D.2    Restricted Decoding with Bounded Space
We first justify the restricted subcode decoder used by the batching tree. For a fixed query direction
and each block, sort the allowed block points by their inner product with that direction. During
enumeration in depth first order, a prefix is visited only when its current score plus the maximum
contribution from every unassigned block can still reach the cap threshold. The children of a prefix
are scanned in sorted order, so scanning stops after the first infeasible child.
     Every feasible prefix has at least one output completion. Charge it to its lexicographically
first output completion. At each depth, an output receives at most one charge, and every feasible
parent incurs at most one additional test of an infeasible child. Hence the traversal visits O(m(1 +
|DecodeD (z)|)) prefixes after sorting. Sorting and forming the rotated block coordinates costs
poly(d)Bpc time and space. This proves Theorem 4.2(i) for every Cartesian subcode, not only for
the root code.
